title: Used Car Market Analysis
description: Explainable ML benchmark for UK used-car listing prices (DVM-CAR, 2012–2021): compared four model families, tuned XGBoost to a £1,037 test MAE, and explained price drivers with SHAP.

details.heading: Project Overview
details.body: Explainable machine-learning analysis of the UK used-car market, built on the DVM-CAR dataset of 268,255 advertisements from 2012–2021. The project benchmarks historical listing prices from observable vehicle characteristics, compares four model families, and explains what drives the estimated prices — published as a reproducible Python project on GitHub.

details.heading: Business Problem
details.body: Consumers often receive vehicle valuations without understanding the factors behind them, and automotive salespeople need to give customers an evidence-based price expectation before a formal trade-in appraisal is available.
points: Goal: an explainable model that estimates used-car listing prices from observable vehicle characteristics and identifies the primary drivers behind those estimates.
Scope boundary kept explicit: the data observe advertised asking prices only — not transaction prices — and exclude condition, accident history, location, and seller type.

details.heading: Approach & Analysis
details.body: Built an end-to-end, reproducible Python workflow (prepare_dataset.py, train_models.py, tune_xgboost.py, analyze_saved_model.py): cleaned and joined the DVM-CAR tables into a 223,104-record core dataset covering 60 makes and 581 models, then engineered 21 predictors including vehicle age, log mileage, and the model-year entry-level new-car price.
points: Leakage-safe preprocessing: missing prices recovered only from the same Adv_ID; train-fitted median imputation applied after the split; stratified random 80/10/10 train/validation/test split.

Compared Ridge, Random Forest, CatBoost, and XGBoost; tuned four XGBoost configurations on validation data only, then refit the selected deep_regularized configuration (1,200 trees, depth 10, learning rate 0.04) on 90% of the data.
Explained predictions with grouped SHAP attribution globally and within Entry, Mainstream, Premium, and Luxury segments, plus standardized 3-year and 5-year residual-value scenarios.

details.heading: Key Findings & Results
details.body: The tuned XGBoost benchmark reached a £1,037 test MAE — about 65 of 100 estimates within 10% and 80 within 15% of the observed listing price — with age, original new-car price, and mileage as the dominant drivers.
points: Top price drivers (mean |SHAP| on log price): vehicle age (0.4169), entry-level new-car price (0.3646), mileage (0.1769), and engine power (0.0790).
Driver rankings shift by segment: vehicle age leads in the Mainstream segment (0.4134), while entry-level new-car price dominates Luxury (1.2021).

Standardized residual-value scenarios highlight strong historical retention for Ferrari (98.5% at 3 years), Dacia, Lamborghini, Porsche, and Land Rover, led by models such as the Ferrari 488 and Porsche 718 Boxster.

details.heading: Business Recommendations
details.body: Positioned as a starting point for pricing conversations — not a replacement for inspection or professional appraisal.
points: Consumers: use the benchmark as an initial historical price reference and review age, mileage, original entry-level price, and condition before buying.
Salespeople: explain Mainstream vehicles mainly through age and mileage; for Premium and Luxury vehicles, also emphasize original price and specification.
Resale-focused buyers: use the 3-year and 5-year residual-value rankings to shortlist vehicles.
Model users: route rare, unseen, or incompletely specified vehicles to human review rather than issuing automated quotes.

title: X5 RetailHero Machine Learning
description: Uplift-modeling case study on X5 RetailHero data: a capacity-aware messaging strategy comparing propensity, uplift, and value-weighted targeting across outreach capacities.

details.heading: Project Overview
details.body: Uplift-modeling case study on the X5 RetailHero competition data, reframed as a customer-operations and sales-strategy problem: not only who is likely to purchase, but how a marketing-operations team should allocate limited outreach capacity across customers with different expected response and historical value. Built on 200,039 labeled customers and roughly 45.8 million product-line purchase records, published as a reproducible Python project on GitHub.

details.heading: Business Problem
details.body: Given customer profiles, pre-campaign transaction history, and campaign response data, how should an operations team allocate limited marketing-outreach resources among customers with different expected response and historical value?
points: Distinguishes three related ideas: gross observed-purchase propensity (who may buy), estimated incremental response (who responds to messaging), and historical-value-weighted uplift (who is also commercially valuable).

Audience: CRM and membership teams, marketing and sales operations teams allocating low-cost scalable vs. high-cost personalized channels, and decision-makers needing a roadmap from response modeling to GMV and ROI.
The observed outcome is a binary post-campaign purchase flag; the value proxy is pre-campaign spend, since post-campaign revenue, margin, and campaign costs are unavailable in the data.

details.heading: Approach & Analysis
details.body: Built a reproducible Python workflow (data audit, feature engineering, modeling, tuning, strategy analysis) on an 80/10/10 train/validation/final-test split of the 200,039 labeled customers, jointly stratified by treatment and outcome. Model selection used validation customers only, with a single final evaluation on the untouched 20,004-customer final-test set.
points: Engineered 17 pre-campaign features from ~117 days of purchase history — spend, frequency, basket value, recency, cadence, consistency, product and category breadth, tenure — de-duplicating receipts at client + transaction grain.
RQ1: compared three XGBoost-based propensity configurations, then ran a pre-specified 24-configuration validation-only tuning search.
RQ2: a T-Learner (one XGBoost model per treatment/control group) estimates incremental response as p_treat − p_control, selected on validation AUUC.
RQ3: compared propensity, uplift-only, and value × uplift ranking rules at equal outreach capacity from 5% to 100%, plus a four-quadrant value/uplift segmentation.

details.heading: Key Findings & Results
details.body: The tuned propensity model reached 0.7787 ROC-AUC on the final test, while the T-Learner identified customer segments with far larger incremental response than the population average — and showed that the highest-propensity customers are not automatically the best messaging targets.
points: Top 10% by uplift rank showed a 9.27 percentage-point observed incremental purchase rate (55.22% treated vs. 45.95% control), vs. 3.33pp across the full final-test population.

At the same top-10% capacity, gross propensity showed no positive incremental effect (−1.25pp), uplift-only delivered 9.27pp, and value-weighted uplift traded response (5.75pp) to target customers with ~2.75× higher mean historical value.
High-propensity customers are frequent, recently active, established shoppers; high-uplift customers have comparatively lower spend and frequency — the two rankings are materially different.
Up to ~30% outreach capacity, uplift-only is the preferred rule; above 40% capacity, no single ranking rule consistently dominates.
Four-quadrant segmentation: Strategic Priority 20.3%, Growth Opportunity 29.8%, Organic High-Value 30.2%, and Low Priority 19.7% of the final-test population.

details.heading: Business Recommendations
details.body: The deliverable is a capacity-aware targeting roadmap rather than a single contact list: define the campaign KPI, channel cost, and outreach capacity first, then choose the ranking rule and channel.
points: For low-cost scalable channels with capacity up to ~30%: rank customers by predicted uplift to maximize additional purchasers per contact.

For high-cost, scarce, or personalized channels: prioritize the Strategic Priority quadrant (high historical value + high uplift), and avoid unnecessary subsidies for high-propensity, low-uplift customers.
Suppress or deprioritize the Low Priority quadrant (19.7% of the test population) from promotional messaging, or move it to very low-cost channels.

Roadmap to profit-based messaging: retain comparable control groups and collect campaign-window GMV, margin, incentive, and channel-cost data to move from purchase response to expected incremental profit.
